questions.q: What is a plugin?
questions.explain: A plugin extends the host through an interface the host defines. The host does not need to change when a new plugin, like a Slack or audit-log plugin, is added.
options: A required part of the application that is always loaded
Code that adds an optional feature to an application through a fixed interface, without changing the application
A copy of the application for one customer
A test helper that replaces real services

questions.q: What is the difference between a runtime module and a plugin?
questions.explain: The difference is who writes the code and who decides to load it. Your modules are always there. Plugins are chosen per installation, so customers only run code for the features they use.
options: Modules are written in TypeScript, plugins in JavaScript
A module is always part of your app; a plugin is optional, may come from another team or npm, and each installation decides whether to load it
Plugins cannot have dependencies, modules can
There is no difference; the words mean the same thing

questions.q: In the plugin system, what is the host?
questions.explain: createPluginContext({ name: "task-api", ... }) describes the host and the services it offers to plugins: a logger, config, a container and events.
options: The server machine that runs Node.js
The npm registry that stores plugins
The application that loads the plugins, here the Task API
The first plugin that was registered

questions.q: A plugin starts a setInterval but never clears it. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: The manager cannot know about your timers. Register the cleanup with context.onDispose(() => clearInterval(timer)), so disposing the plugin really stops its work.
options: Nothing: manager.stop clears all timers automatically
The interval keeps the process alive forever and keeps running after the plugin was "stopped"
The interval runs only once
The plugin cannot be registered

It is an AbortSignal that fires when the plugin system shuts down, to cancel slow work such as a fetch
It tells the plugin which version of the host is running
It sends events to other plugins

questions.q: Why does the reminder plugin check options.everyMs in install and throw when it is wrong?
questions.explain: An interval of 0 ms or "40" as text would misbehave quietly for a long time. Failing at start-up shows the mistake at once.
options: TypeScript cannot check options
Settings from outside are input like any other; a wrong value should stop the start-up, not cause strange behaviour later
Throwing in install makes the plugin faster
So the plugin is skipped silently

questions.q: Why does manager.start roll back when one plugin's hook throws?
questions.explain: On a failed start, the manager stops and disposes every plugin it had already brought up, then throws the error to you. Nothing is left running.
options: To try the failing plugin again
Half-started plugins are dangerous: some timers run and connections are open, and nothing would ever stop them
To delete the plugin from npm
Rollback is only for database plugins

questions.q: Why does the Task API's event hub wrap each handler call in try/catch?
questions.explain: The request that completes a task should not fail because a plugin's audit or Slack handler threw. The hub catches the error and reports it to onError, where the host logs it.
options: To make handlers run faster
So a broken plugin handler cannot break the request that emitted the event
So errors are sent to the client
Because emit must return a value

questions.q: The audit-log plugin only uses context.events and context.logger. What is the benefit?
questions.explain: The plugin and the host only share the plugin interface. You can add Slack, statistics or reminder plugins without touching the host, except for one register line.
options: It runs faster than a plugin that imports the Task API
It works in any host that offers events and a logger, and the host only needs to know the plugin interface
It can read every environment variable safely
It does not need a name

questions.q: The Slack plugin needs a secret webhook address. What does the Task API do?
questions.explain: Secrets never go into code or metadata. The host reads SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL and simply does not register the plugin when it is missing, instead of failing or leaking a secret.
options: Write the address in the plugin's source code
Put the address in the plugin's metadata
Read it from an environment variable; when it is missing, log a warning and start without the Slack plugin
Ask the client to send it in a header

questions.q: A host sets allowedCapabilities: ["events"]. Can a hostile plugin still read process.env and send your data anywhere?
questions.explain: Plugins run in your process with all its rights. Only install plugins you trust, pin their versions and review what they do, exactly as with any other npm dependency.
options: No: the manager blocks every capability that is not granted
Yes: capabilities are a declaration that catches mistakes, not a sandbox; plugins are ordinary code in your process
No, because plugins run in a separate process
Only if the plugin is written in TypeScript

questions.q: Why should a plugin package export a factory like createAuditLogPlugin() instead of a ready-made plugin object?
questions.explain: A shared object would share its state, like a counter or a timer, between hosts and tests. A disposed object also cannot be started again; a factory simply makes a new one.
options: npm refuses to publish plain objects
Every host, and every test, gets a fresh plugin with fresh state
Factories are required by TypeScript
So the plugin can never be disposed

questions.q: Why does a published plugin list @zudojs/plugins in peerDependencies instead of dependencies?
questions.explain: A peer dependency says "the host must provide this". One shared copy keeps instanceof checks working. List it in devDependencies too, so you can build and test.
options: Peer dependencies install faster
The host must provide it; with a copy per plugin, classes like PluginDependencyError from one copy fail instanceof against another
Peer dependencies are never downloaded
So users cannot see which version the plugin needs

questions.q: Why does the plugin use import type { Plugin } from "@zudojs/plugins" where it can?
questions.explain: A type-only import is removed when TypeScript compiles. The plugin then does not load its own copy of @zudojs/plugins at runtime.
options: Type imports make the package larger
Type imports disappear from the compiled code, so the plugin works with whatever copy of the package the host has
Normal imports are not allowed in plugins
So TypeScript skips checking the plugin

questions.q: The package.json has "files": ["dist"]. What does npm pack --dry-run show will be uploaded?
questions.explain: files lists what to ship. Your source, node_modules and any .env file stay at home. Always check with npm pack --dry-run before npm publish.
options: Everything in the folder, including src, node_modules and .env
The compiled dist files plus package.json and the README, which npm always adds
Only package.json
Only the TypeScript source files

questions.q: What helps other people find your plugin on npm?
questions.explain: Keywords in package.json are searchable on npm. You can only publish under a scope you own, like @acme, not @zudojs.
options: Putting the word "plugin" in every file name
The keyword zudojs-plugin in package.json
Publishing it under the @zudojs scope
A very high version number
